screens.title: Managing and Querying Private Data Collections
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn the practical patterns for submitting private inputs to chaincode, retrieving raw private data when you are a collection member, and verifying private data using hashes on the public ledger. We will connect the client-side responsibilities — preparing transient maps and matching keys expected by GetTransient — with on-chain behaviors like GetPrivateData and GetPrivateDataHash. You will also see the implications of retention settings such as blockToLive, and how auditing and off-chain archives fit into a production strategy. Concrete examples include a Node. js SDK snippet that attaches transient data, and a CLI lab that demonstrates base64-encoding transient payloads, invoking CreateAssetWithPrivateDetails, querying as an authorized peer, and verifying the private data hash from any member. By the end, you’ll understand not only the code calls to use, but the security and operational trade-offs when designing private data collections. Consider how the hash on the public ledger can serve as immutable proof even after raw data is purged.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you will use when building client-side logic and operating private data collections. First, you will learn to construct transaction proposals that include private inputs, formatting them as transient data and converting JSON payloads into Buffer or base64-encoded transient entries as required by the SDK or CLI. Second, you will practice querying private data from authorized peers, using chaincode functions that call GetPrivateData and understanding why only collection members can access raw values. Third, you will learn to query private data hashes from the main ledger; this allows verification by non-members without revealing secrets. And fourth, you will start a CLI-based lab that walks through encoding, invoking CreateAssetWithPrivateDetails, and validating responses. Each objective links a concrete action to why it matters in production: confidentiality, auditability, and reproducible verification.

screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on reliability, auditability, and policy. First, you will understand the impact of blockToLive in collection_config. json, how it causes private data to be purged after a number of blocks, and why the public hash persists. Each objective pairs a clear task with real operational reasons for doing it.

screens.title: Submitting Private Data via Transient Inputs
screens.narratorSegment: A client must treat private inputs differently from public transaction arguments. Transient data is a transient map attached to the proposal: it bypasses the ordering service and is delivered only to endorsing peers and the chaincode. The critical development steps are: stringify your JSON, convert it to a Buffer when using SDKs, or base64-encode it for the CLI, and use a transient key name that exactly matches what the chaincode’s GetTransient expects. In practice you will see patterns such as setTransient in the Node. js SDK or the --transient flag on the peer CLI. A concrete example is preparing an asset object, converting it to Buffer, and calling setTransient with key asset_private_details. A common misconception is to put secrets in the Args array or public state; that exposes them to the orderer and all peers. Always verify that your transient key names match chaincode and that your application handles endorsement errors when a required private endorsement is not satisfied. The takeaway: use transient data to preserve confidentiality while still allowing chaincode logic to process secret inputs. Submitting Private Data via Transient Inputs means stringify private json, buffer or base64 encode, and place in the transient map with the chaincode-expected key to keep secrets out of the orderer.. In practical terms, how clients attach private payloads so that only endorsers and chaincode see secrets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Transient submissions
keyIdea.text: Stringify private JSON, Buffer or base64 encode, and place in the transient map with the chaincode-expected key to keep secrets out of the orderer.

content.html:
Core Concept
Submitting private inputs
Prepare and attach transient data so only endorsers and chaincode receive secrets. Avoid putting secrets in public args.
Node.js SDK example (visual)
// conceptual snippet (visual)
const privateDetails = {"ID":"asset100","Price":1500,"Secret":"confidential-info-xyz"};
const privateDetailsBuffer = Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(privateDetails));
const transientMap = { asset_private_details: privateDetailsBuffer };
await contract.createTransaction('CreateAssetWithPrivateDetails')
  .setTransient(transientMap)
  .submit();
Note: the key asset_private_details must match chaincode GetTransient expectations. The Buffer is not serialized to the ordering service.
Checklist
  • JSON stringify private objects, then Buffer (SDK) or base64 (CLI).
  • Use matching transient key names expected by chaincode GetTransient.
  • Do not place secrets in the Args array or public state keys.
  • Handle endorsement failures due to missing private endorsements.
Common mistake
Putting private values in regular Args exposes them to the orderer and all peers. Use transient fields instead.
Key Takeaway

Transient data keeps secret inputs out of the orderer; match keys and encoding to chaincode expectations to ensure confidentiality.

screens.title: What is Transient Data?
screens.narratorSegment: Transient data is a proposal-scoped map of key-value pairs that accompany a transaction proposal but are explicitly excluded from the ordering service. Conceptually, think of transient data as private input that endorsers and chaincode can use to compute state, but which is not recorded on the public ledger. This property matters because it protects highly sensitive fields like prices, secrets, or personally identifiable information while still enabling the chaincode to compute and store a hash on the public ledger for verification. For example, you may include an invoice secret in transient data so endorsers can validate and compute an appraised value, then publish only a hash in the public asset record. A common misconception is that transient data is stored long-term on peers; it is not part of the ordered ledger and therefore not retained by the ordering service. However, endorsing peers may temporarily use it to create private writes. Always design to avoid assuming transient inputs persist beyond the endorsement and commit process. What is Transient Data? means transient data travels to endorsers and chaincode only; it never passes through the orderer and should not be treated as persisted ledger data.. In practical terms, a precise definition and why it matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
Transient Data
A proposal-scoped private map delivered only to endorsers and chaincode, excluded from ordering and public ledger storage.
Why it matters
  • Protects sensitive inputs while allowing chaincode to compute results.
  • Enables publishing only hashes to the public ledger for auditing.
  • Prevents the orderer and non-endorsing peers from seeing secret content.
Analogy
Think of transient data as a sealed envelope shown only to specific notaries who sign a public receipt instead of publishing the letter itself.
Misconception
Transient data is not stored on the public ledger; do not expect it to persist across peer restarts or after retention policies purge private stores.
Key Takeaway

Use transient inputs to keep secrets private and publish only derived hashes publicly for verification.

screens.narratorSegment: The CLI lab demonstrates the concrete steps to send transient data using the peer command. First, prepare your private JSON and base64-encode it. This encoding is necessary because the CLI transient flag expects a serialized value. A common error is forgetting to pass the same transient key string the chaincode expects. keyIdea.title: CLI pattern
keyIdea.text: Base64 the JSON, export TRANSIENT_DATA, and invoke peer chaincode with --transient using the exact key name the chaincode expects.

content.html:
Process Flow
CLI: prepare & invoke
Base64-encode private JSON then call peer chaincode invoke with the --transient flag set to the encoded value.
Terminal steps (visual)
# Prepare transient data
PRIVATE_DETAILS='{"ID":"asset1","Price":1200,"Secret":"invoice-123-ABC"}'
export TRANSIENT_DATA=$(echo -n "${PRIVATE_DETAILS}" | base64 | tr -d \'\
\')

# Invoke with transient (Org1 context)
peer chaincode invoke -C mychannel -n asset-private --transient "{\"asset_private_details\":\"${TRANSIENT_DATA}\"}" -c '{"Args":["CreateAssetWithPrivateDetails"]}'
Checklist
  • Encode JSON using base64 for the CLI.
  • Ensure setGlobalsCLI or equivalent environment context for the invoking org.
  • Provide peerAddresses and tlsRootCertFiles for multi-org invocations.
  • Match transient key name exactly to chaincode GetTransient key.
Expected outcome
Successful invocation; private payload sent only to endorsers. Public state may contain a PrivateHash value for verification.
Key Takeaway

Use base64 for CLI transient values and verify the chaincode key name to ensure the secret reaches endorsers only.

screens.title: Querying Private Data as a Collection Member
screens.narratorSegment: When your application acts as a member of a private data collection, it can retrieve the raw private content by sending a proposal to an endorsing peer that is in that collection. The chaincode should implement a ReadPrivateAssetDetails function that calls GetPrivateData(collectionName, key) and returns the stored JSON. Using an SDK you would call evaluateTransaction('ReadPrivateAssetDetails', 'asset100') and parse the returned buffer. With the peer CLI you simply run peer chaincode query for that function under an environment context for a member organization. A common problem is querying a peer that has not yet received the private payload via gossip; the result may be empty even for a member immediately after commit. Also implement error handling for empty responses to indicate either non-membership or gossip delay. Practically, verify the peer’s membership in the collection, and if immediate consistency is required, consider application-level retries or querying multiple endorsing peers. The key point is only collection members can see raw private data; others cannot. Querying Private Data as a Collection Member means use getprivatedata from a collection member peer; handle empty results and gossip eventual consistency by checking membership and retrying when necessary.. In practical terms, how to retrieve raw private values from a peer that holds the collection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use GetPrivateData from a collection member peer; handle empty results and gossip eventual consistency by checking membership and retrying when necessary.

content.html:
Process Flow
Query raw private data
Clients must target a peer that is a member of the private collection and call a chaincode function using GetPrivateData.
SDK example (visual)
const resultBuffer = await contract.evaluateTransaction('ReadPrivateAssetDetails', 'asset100');
const privateDetails = JSON.parse(resultBuffer.toString());
If the peer does not hold the private data or gossip hasn't delivered it, you may get an empty result or an error.
Operational notes
  • Ensure the target peer is a collection member.
  • Expect eventual consistency from gossip; implement retry logic when necessary.
  • Log and surface authorization errors distinctly from empty results.
Example scenario
Org1 queries ReadPrivateAssetDetails for asset1 and receives the JSON with Price and Secret because Org1 is a collection member.
Key Takeaway

Only collection members can fetch raw private data. Account for gossip delays and implement clear error handling for missing data.

screens.title: Private Data vs Private Data Hash
screens.narratorSegment: It helps to compare raw private data access with access to a private data hash. Collection members calling GetPrivateData receive the full JSON payload. Non-members cannot retrieve that content; their attempt will typically return empty or an error. However, any channel member can call GetPrivateDataHash for a specific collection name and key; that returns a cryptographic hash stored on the public ledger. The hash enables verification without disclosing secrets. For example, after a private CreateAssetWithPrivateDetails transaction, the public asset can contain a PrivateHash field. A verifier provides the same private payload as transient input to a verification function that computes the hash and compares it to the ledger value. This pattern supports auditability: even if blockToLive later purges the raw data, the hash remains as immutable proof. A common false assumption is that the hash reveals the private content; it does not. It only proves consistency and existence when a valid preimage is presented. Private Data vs Private Data Hash means members get raw data via getprivatedata; all channel members can verify existence and integrity using getprivatedatahash without seeing the secret itself.. In practical terms, what members and non-members can access and why the hash matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Members get raw data via GetPrivateData; all channel members can verify existence and integrity using GetPrivateDataHash without seeing the secret itself.

content.html:
Comparison
Raw Private Data
Accessible only to collection members via GetPrivateData. Returns the actual JSON payload stored in the private state database.
Example
Org1 queries ReadPrivateAssetDetails and receives {"ID":"asset1","Price":1200,"Secret":"invoice-123-ABC"}.
Comparison
Private Data Hash
Stored on the public ledger and retrievable via GetPrivateDataHash. Use it to verify that a private payload matches an on-chain record without revealing the payload itself.
Verification pattern
Provide the private payload as transient input and run a chaincode verifier that computes its hash and compares it to the ledger's PrivateHash. Expected output: true if matched.
Key Takeaway

Hash on the ledger provides immutable proof without exposing secrets; combine it with transient verification to audit private data.

Misconception
A hash does not disclose the payload content; it only permits checking whether a provided payload matches the recorded hash.
Practical tip
Keep the verification routine lightweight: compute the hash and compare to the public ledger entry for fast audits.

screens.title: blockToLive and Data Retention
screens.narratorSegment: The blockToLive parameter in collection_config. json defines how many blocks of the channel ledger a piece of private data should be retained on collection members before automatic purging. If you set blockToLive to a non-zero value, raw private data will be removed from the private data store after that many blocks have been appended. Crucially, the public ledger still retains the hash of the private data permanently. This means GetPrivateData calls will fail or return empty after purge, while GetPrivateDataHash calls continue to succeed. Operationally this impacts audits: you can prove that private data existed by presenting the original payload and comparing hashes, but you cannot retrieve the raw content from peers after purge unless you have an off-chain archive. A common operational mistake is assuming private data will be available indefinitely; plan your archival and compliance strategy accordingly. If long-term access is needed, implement secure off-chain backups that are linked to on-chain hashes, and ensure access controls and encryption for those archives. blockToLive and Data Retention means blocktolive controls automatic purging of raw private data after n blocks; the hash remains on the public ledger to support verification.. In practical terms, how retention settings affect private data availability and auditing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: blockToLive controls automatic purging of raw private data after N blocks; the hash remains on the public ledger to support verification.

content.html:
Definition
Data Retention: blockToLive
blockToLive determines how many ledger blocks private data persists on a peer before the private store purges it. The public hash remains for auditing.
Implications
  • After blockToLive expires, GetPrivateData will return empty or fail.
  • GetPrivateDataHash still works and provides immutable proof of prior existence.
  • Plan off-chain archival if raw data must be available past retention.
Operational example
If blockToLive is 100 and 150 blocks have passed, the private data is purged and cannot be retrieved from peers, but the ledger still shows the stored hash.
Key Takeaway

Use on-chain hashes for proof and off-chain archives when you need persistent access to raw private data beyond blockToLive limits.

screens.title: Endorsement Policies for Private Data Collections
screens.narratorSegment: Private data collections have their own endorsement rules defined in collection_config. json. These rules determine which peers must endorse writes that modify the collection. Importantly, collection endorsement is separate from the chaincode endorsement policy for public state. When a transaction writes to a private collection, endorsers specified by the collection’s endorsementPolicy must produce matching results; otherwise endorsement will fail. This affects client behavior: your application must send proposals to the required endorsing peers and include their endorsements when submitting the transaction. A typical pitfall is testing transactions against only a single peer when the collection policy requires multiple organizational endorsements. In such a case the ordering will reject the transaction because endorsements are incomplete. For robust operations, identify which peers are required for each collection, design client logic to gather endorsements from them, and surface clear error messages when a required endorsement is missing. This ensures privacy boundaries are respected while preserving correctness. Endorsement Policies for Private Data Collections means collection-level endorsementpolicy defines which peers must endorse private writes; clients must collect those endorsements prior to submission.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Endorsement policies for PDCs
Collection endorsement policies declare which organizations or peers must endorse writes to the private collection, influencing how clients gather endorsements.
Client responsibilities

screens.title: Verification Pattern: Provide Private Data as Transient Input
screens.narratorSegment: Verification uses the same transient patterns to prove possession of private data. The verifier prepares the private payload as transient data and calls a chaincode function like VerifyPrivateAssetDetails. The chaincode computes the hash of the transient payload and compares it to the PrivateHash stored on the public ledger via GetPrivateDataHash. The function returns a boolean indicating whether the provided private input matches the ledger hash. This enables any channel member to confirm integrity without accessing raw private stores. In practice, you will supply the same JSON used during creation as a transient input and run the verify function; if the chaincode returns true, you have cryptographic proof that the payload matched the original that produced the hash. A misconception is thinking verification requires the private data to be on the verifying peer; it does not. The verifying peer only needs the hash on the ledger and the provided transient payload for the comparison. keyIdea.text: Provide the private payload as transient input; chaincode computes its hash and compares it to the public ledger's private hash to verify integrity.

Process Flow
Verification with transient input
Supply the private payload transiently and let chaincode compare its computed hash against the ledger-stored hash to confirm integrity.
Step 1
Prepare private payload and base64 or Buffer encode as required.
Step 2
Call VerifyPrivateAssetDetails providing the transient map with the payload.
Step 3
Chaincode computes hash and compares it to the ledger value returned by GetPrivateDataHash, returning true or false.

Verification proves possession without exposing raw private storage. The verifier needs the ledger hash and a candidate preimage as transient input.

screens.title: Common Challenges, Performance, and Gossip
screens.narratorSegment: Private data distribution relies on Fabric’s gossip protocol, which provides eventual consistency for private collections. This can create short windows where a member peer has not yet received the private payload after commit, causing immediate queries to return empty. To address this, implement client-side retry strategies and prefer querying multiple endorsers when possible. Performance can also be affected by large collection sizes and high requiredPeerCount values; tune collection size and retention to match your privacy and throughput needs. Another challenge is the added latency of private data gossip compared to public state updates, so design user-facing pipelines to tolerate short delays or confirm transaction completion via events and then query private data. For auditing, combine ledger hashes with secure off-chain backups if you need long-term raw access. Finally, log and monitor failed GetPrivateData calls separately so operators can diagnose membership, gossip health, and retention-related issues quickly. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Expect eventual consistency for private data via gossip; add retries, monitor gossip health, and design retention and collection sizes to balance privacy and throughput.

content.html:
Core Concept
Gossip, consistency, and performance
Understand the trade-offs of private data distribution and design clients to handle eventual consistency and performance considerations.
Issue
A newly committed private write may not be immediately available on all member peers due to gossip latency.
Mitigation
Implement retries, query multiple endorsers, and wait for commit events before fetching private data.
Performance tip
Tune collection sizes and requiredPeerCount to balance privacy needs with gossip and endorsement latency.
Operational warning
Treat missing GetPrivateData results as operational signals: membership, gossip health, or retention may be the cause rather than bad data.
Key Takeaway

Design for eventual consistency: use retries, monitor gossip, and plan collection sizes and retention to meet both privacy and performance goals.

screens.title: Auditing Private Data and Off-Chain Archival
screens.narratorSegment: Because blockToLive can remove raw private data from peers, a robust audit strategy often combines the ledger-stored hash with secure off-chain archival of raw private payloads. The ledger hash provides immutable proof a record existed and what its digest was at commit time. For long-term audits you should: store encrypted off-chain copies of private data, keep metadata linking each archive entry to the on-chain PrivateHash, restrict access to archives with strong access controls, and log retrieval events for compliance. During an audit a verifier presents the archived payload, the chaincode verifies the hash matches the ledger entry, and the auditor can confirm integrity even if peers have purged raw data. Be careful to protect off-chain archives at least as well as on-chain private stores: leaks in the archive defeat the purpose of PDCs. The operational cost of archival must be balanced with compliance requirements and the retention choices made in collection_config. json. Auditing Private Data and Off-Chain Archival means combine immutable on-chain hashes with secure, access-controlled off-chain archives to enable long-term auditing when blocktolive purges private data.. In practical terms, designing audits that survive blocktolive purges. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Audit strategy
keyIdea.text: Combine immutable on-chain hashes with secure, access-controlled off-chain archives to enable long-term auditing when blockToLive purges private data.

content.html:
Best Practice
Auditing and Off-Chain Archival
Use on-chain hashes as immutable anchors while storing encrypted off-chain archives for raw private data that must survive retention purges.
Audit flow
  1. Store encrypted private payload off-chain with metadata including PrivateHash.
  2. On audit, present payload; run verification to match hash to ledger.
  3. Log verification events and access to archives for compliance.
Archive guidance
Encrypt archives, use strict access controls, rotate keys, and maintain tamper-evident logs to preserve confidentiality and prove integrity.
Key Takeaway

Plan archival and verification procedures ahead of deployment so audits remain possible even after blockToLive purges raw private data.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn the practical patterns for submitting private inputs to chaincode, retrieving raw private data when you are a collection member, and verifying private data using hashes on the public ledger. We will connect the client-side responsibilities — preparing transient maps and matching keys expected by GetTransient — with on-chain behaviors like GetPrivateData and GetPrivateDataHash. You will also see the implications of retention settings such as blockToLive, and how auditing and off-chain archives fit into a production strategy. Concrete examples include a Node. js SDK snippet that attaches transient data, and a CLI lab that demonstrates base64-encoding transient payloads, invoking CreateAssetWithPrivateDetails, querying as an authorized peer, and verifying the private data hash from any member. By the end, you’ll understand not only the code calls to use, but the security and operational trade-offs when designing private data collections. Consider how the hash on the public ledger can serve as immutable proof even after raw data is purged.

These objectives map to practical skills you will use when building client-side logic and operating private data collections. First, you will learn to construct transaction proposals that include private inputs, formatting them as transient data and converting JSON payloads into Buffer or base64-encoded transient entries as required by the SDK or CLI. Second, you will practice querying private data from authorized peers, using chaincode functions that call GetPrivateData and understanding why only collection members can access raw values. Third, you will learn to query private data hashes from the main ledger; this allows verification by non-members without revealing secrets. And fourth, you will start a CLI-based lab that walks through encoding, invoking CreateAssetWithPrivateDetails, and validating responses. Each objective links a concrete action to why it matters in production: confidentiality, auditability, and reproducible verification.

These objectives focus on reliability, auditability, and policy. First, you will understand the impact of blockToLive in collection_config. json, how it causes private data to be purged after a number of blocks, and why the public hash persists. Second, you will learn client-side best practices: matching transient keys to GetTransient expectations, handling Buffer or base64 encoding, and implementing robust error handling for unauthorized or missing data. Third, you will explore endorsementPolicy nuances for private data collections and how required peers and endorsement rules influence which endorsements are necessary to write private data. Finally, you will design an auditing strategy that ties on-chain hashes to an off-chain archival approach when long-term access to raw private data is needed. Each objective pairs a clear task with real operational reasons for doing it.

A client must treat private inputs differently from public transaction arguments. Transient data is a transient map attached to the proposal: it bypasses the ordering service and is delivered only to endorsing peers and the chaincode. The critical development steps are: stringify your JSON, convert it to a Buffer when using SDKs, or base64-encode it for the CLI, and use a transient key name that exactly matches what the chaincode’s GetTransient expects. In practice you will see patterns such as setTransient in the Node. js SDK or the --transient flag on the peer CLI. A concrete example is preparing an asset object, converting it to Buffer, and calling setTransient with key asset_private_details. A common misconception is to put secrets in the Args array or public state; that exposes them to the orderer and all peers. Always verify that your transient key names match chaincode and that your application handles endorsement errors when a required private endorsement is not satisfied. The takeaway: use transient data to preserve confidentiality while still allowing chaincode logic to process secret inputs. Submitting Private Data via Transient Inputs means stringify private json, buffer or base64 encode, and place in the transient map with the chaincode-expected key to keep secrets out of the orderer.. In practical terms, how clients attach private payloads so that only endorsers and chaincode see secrets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Transient data is a proposal-scoped map of key-value pairs that accompany a transaction proposal but are explicitly excluded from the ordering service. Conceptually, think of transient data as private input that endorsers and chaincode can use to compute state, but which is not recorded on the public ledger. This property matters because it protects highly sensitive fields like prices, secrets, or personally identifiable information while still enabling the chaincode to compute and store a hash on the public ledger for verification. For example, you may include an invoice secret in transient data so endorsers can validate and compute an appraised value, then publish only a hash in the public asset record. A common misconception is that transient data is stored long-term on peers; it is not part of the ordered ledger and therefore not retained by the ordering service. However, endorsing peers may temporarily use it to create private writes. Always design to avoid assuming transient inputs persist beyond the endorsement and commit process. What is Transient Data? means transient data travels to endorsers and chaincode only; it never passes through the orderer and should not be treated as persisted ledger data.. In practical terms, a precise definition and why it matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The CLI lab demonstrates the concrete steps to send transient data using the peer command. First, prepare your private JSON and base64-encode it. This encoding is necessary because the CLI transient flag expects a serialized value. Next, set the environment to the org whose peer participates in the collection and invoke the chaincode with --transient and the matching transient key. In practice you will export a TRANSIENT_DATA variable that contains the base64 payload and then use peer chaincode invoke with --transient '{"asset_private_details":" "}'. The transaction will be sent to the orderer without the secret content; only endorsing peers in the collection will receive the private payload. A common error is forgetting to pass the same transient key string the chaincode expects. Another pitfall is not including both required peerAddresses and tlsRootCertFiles when invoking across organizations. After submission check the invocation response for success and verify that a PrivateHash appears in the public asset if chaincode writes it. This walkthrough prepares you to run the hands-on activity step by step. CLI Walkthrough: Encoding and Invoking with --transient means base64 the json, export transient_data, and invoke peer chaincode with --transient using the exact key name the chaincode expects.. In practical terms, terminal-first steps to submit a private asset using the peer cli. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When your application acts as a member of a private data collection, it can retrieve the raw private content by sending a proposal to an endorsing peer that is in that collection. The chaincode should implement a ReadPrivateAssetDetails function that calls GetPrivateData(collectionName, key) and returns the stored JSON. Using an SDK you would call evaluateTransaction('ReadPrivateAssetDetails', 'asset100') and parse the returned buffer. With the peer CLI you simply run peer chaincode query for that function under an environment context for a member organization. A common problem is querying a peer that has not yet received the private payload via gossip; the result may be empty even for a member immediately after commit. Also implement error handling for empty responses to indicate either non-membership or gossip delay. Practically, verify the peer’s membership in the collection, and if immediate consistency is required, consider application-level retries or querying multiple endorsing peers. The key point is only collection members can see raw private data; others cannot. Querying Private Data as a Collection Member means use getprivatedata from a collection member peer; handle empty results and gossip eventual consistency by checking membership and retrying when necessary.. In practical terms, how to retrieve raw private values from a peer that holds the collection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

It helps to compare raw private data access with access to a private data hash. Collection members calling GetPrivateData receive the full JSON payload. Non-members cannot retrieve that content; their attempt will typically return empty or an error. However, any channel member can call GetPrivateDataHash for a specific collection name and key; that returns a cryptographic hash stored on the public ledger. The hash enables verification without disclosing secrets. For example, after a private CreateAssetWithPrivateDetails transaction, the public asset can contain a PrivateHash field. A verifier provides the same private payload as transient input to a verification function that computes the hash and compares it to the ledger value. This pattern supports auditability: even if blockToLive later purges the raw data, the hash remains as immutable proof. A common false assumption is that the hash reveals the private content; it does not. It only proves consistency and existence when a valid preimage is presented. Private Data vs Private Data Hash means members get raw data via getprivatedata; all channel members can verify existence and integrity using getprivatedatahash without seeing the secret itself.. In practical terms, what members and non-members can access and why the hash matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The blockToLive parameter in collection_config. json defines how many blocks of the channel ledger a piece of private data should be retained on collection members before automatic purging. If you set blockToLive to a non-zero value, raw private data will be removed from the private data store after that many blocks have been appended. Crucially, the public ledger still retains the hash of the private data permanently. This means GetPrivateData calls will fail or return empty after purge, while GetPrivateDataHash calls continue to succeed. Operationally this impacts audits: you can prove that private data existed by presenting the original payload and comparing hashes, but you cannot retrieve the raw content from peers after purge unless you have an off-chain archive. A common operational mistake is assuming private data will be available indefinitely; plan your archival and compliance strategy accordingly. Private data collections have their own endorsement rules defined in collection_config. json. These rules determine which peers must endorse writes that modify the collection. Importantly, collection endorsement is separate from the chaincode endorsement policy for public state. When a transaction writes to a private collection, endorsers specified by the collection’s endorsementPolicy must produce matching results; otherwise endorsement will fail. This affects client behavior: your application must send proposals to the required endorsing peers and include their endorsements when submitting the transaction. A typical pitfall is testing transactions against only a single peer when the collection policy requires multiple organizational endorsements. In such a case the ordering will reject the transaction because endorsements are incomplete. For robust operations, identify which peers are required for each collection, design client logic to gather endorsements from them, and surface clear error messages when a required endorsement is missing. This ensures privacy boundaries are respected while preserving correctness. Verification uses the same transient patterns to prove possession of private data. The verifier prepares the private payload as transient data and calls a chaincode function like VerifyPrivateAssetDetails. The chaincode computes the hash of the transient payload and compares it to the PrivateHash stored on the public ledger via GetPrivateDataHash. The function returns a boolean indicating whether the provided private input matches the ledger hash. This enables any channel member to confirm integrity without accessing raw private stores. In practice, you will supply the same JSON used during creation as a transient input and run the verify function; if the chaincode returns true, you have cryptographic proof that the payload matched the original that produced the hash. A misconception is thinking verification requires the private data to be on the verifying peer; it does not. The verifying peer only needs the hash on the ledger and the provided transient payload for the comparison. Private data distribution relies on Fabric’s gossip protocol, which provides eventual consistency for private collections. This can create short windows where a member peer has not yet received the private payload after commit, causing immediate queries to return empty. To address this, implement client-side retry strategies and prefer querying multiple endorsers when possible. Performance can also be affected by large collection sizes and high requiredPeerCount values; tune collection size and retention to match your privacy and throughput needs. Another challenge is the added latency of private data gossip compared to public state updates, so design user-facing pipelines to tolerate short delays or confirm transaction completion via events and then query private data. For auditing, combine ledger hashes with secure off-chain backups if you need long-term raw access. Finally, log and monitor failed GetPrivateData calls separately so operators can diagnose membership, gossip health, and retention-related issues quickly. Because blockToLive can remove raw private data from peers, a robust audit strategy often combines the ledger-stored hash with secure off-chain archival of raw private payloads. The ledger hash provides immutable proof a record existed and what its digest was at commit time. For long-term audits you should: store encrypted off-chain copies of private data, keep metadata linking each archive entry to the on-chain PrivateHash, restrict access to archives with strong access controls, and log retrieval events for compliance. During an audit a verifier presents the archived payload, the chaincode verifies the hash matches the ledger entry, and the auditor can confirm integrity even if peers have purged raw data. Be careful to protect off-chain archives at least as well as on-chain private stores: leaks in the archive defeat the purpose of PDCs. The operational cost of archival must be balanced with compliance requirements and the retention choices made in collection_config. json.
